title: The usual version. It was not simply pounds against kilograms.
description:
It was not simply pounds against kilograms. The Board of Inquiry called that explanation simplistic and inaccurate. The crew used a factor of 1.77, which converts litres to pounds, where one for kilograms, about 0.8, was needed.

A Boeing 767 needed 22,300 kilograms of fuel. It left with roughly 10,000 kilograms, less than half, and nobody on board knew.

Then both engines failed at 35,000. About 65 miles from Winnipeg and 45 miles from Gimli, a former air force base, according to the Board of Inquiry.

The captain. First Officer Maurice Quintal had once been stationed at Gimli himself, and the pair glided the 767 towards the old base.

Aboard: 61 passengers and 8 crew. Everyone lived. The jet touched down within 800 feet of the threshold of a 7,200 foot runway.

Both engines out. Everyone lived.

Sources:
- https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gimli_Glider: read. Established the 23 July 1983 date, the Boeing 767, 69 people aboard, the 22,300 kg the flight needed, the correct top up of 20,088 litres, the nose gear collapse, and that Gimli was a former RCAF base.
- https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/2024-12/AirCanada143_C-GAUN.pdf: Board of Inquiry report, first 100,000 of about 119,800 characters read. Established that 1.77 is a litres to pounds factor where a litres to kilograms factor (about 0.8) was needed, warnings at 41,000 ft and both engines out at 35,000 ft, about 65 miles from Winnipeg and 45 from Gimli, 61 passengers and 6 cabin crew, no loss of life, a 7,200 ft runway, touchdown within 800 ft of the threshold, and the Board calling a pure metric mix up explanation simplistic and inaccurate.
- https://code7700.com/case_study_air_canada_143.htm: read. Established the 7,682 litre dipstick reading, the 1.77 factor being applied, roughly 4,917 litres ordered, 8 crew and 61 passengers, and that the aircraft was among those with fuel gauges in kilograms while the rest of the fleet used pounds.
- https://www.cbc.ca/archives/when-a-metric-mix-up-led-to-the-gimli-glider-emergency-1.4754039: read. Established Captain Robert Pearson and First Officer Maurice Quintal, Quintal having once been stationed at Gimli, and that part of the old base was in use for racing.
- https://www.aopa.org/news-and-media/all-news/2000/july/pilot/the-gimli-glider: read. Established the landing detail and the skid on the nose after the main tyres blew.
